posts.postCaption: Spent 5 days, 4 nights in Austria…and here’s everything we did ✨ If I were you, allot more time here tho 🙈 The train from Prague to Vienna took around four hours, and we arrived just in time for dinner. Thank God for the long summer days in Europe! The sun set late, we still had plenty of time to stroll through the parks and explore the area around our hotel on foot (and also checked how to go around the train station) Early mornings at Schönbrunn Palace hit different when there are no crowds, just the quiet beauty of Vienna’s most iconic palace. Since we were short on time, we took a horse-drawn carriage ride around the grounds and got to see so much of the palace in the most charming way. We made our way to Naschmarkt for a well-deserved lunch break, then spent the afternoon wandering through the stunning halls of the Kunsthistorisches Museum. A perfect mix of good food, art, and Vienna charm. I was just in awe. Every piece of art drew so much emotion. I can’t help but envy the artists who can create something so timeless 🥺 The following day we picked up our rented car and drove to Salzburg. It started to rain, so I ended up shopping instead 😅 The morning drive to Hallstatt was one of the most beautiful and relaxing parts of our trip: winding roads, mountain views, and the calmest atmosphere. Sadly, the Salt Mine was closed during our visit, but we were still able to see the Beinhaus (Skull House), a small chapel that holds painted skulls dating back centuries. It was created because the village cemetery had limited burial space, and the remains of past residents were carefully preserved and honored there. In the afternoon, we visited the Dom zu Salzburg and were lucky enough to witness a beautiful choir performance. We took a moment to pray and thank God for all the blessings, guidance, and unforgettable experiences this journey has brought us. Afterwards, we visited Hohensalzburg Fortress, one of the largest and best preserved medieval castles in Europe. Built in 1077 by Archbishop Gebhard during the power struggles between the Church and the Holy Roman Empire, the fortress was designed to protect Salzburg and assert the archbishop’s authority.

For 250 years, American Jews have helped shape, challenge, and reimagine the nation's democratic ideals. This powerful exhibition traces Jewish participation in American political life from the Revolutionary era to the present, through rare objects, compelling stories, and voices both renowned and lesser-known, from Emma Lazarus and Henry Morgenthau Jr. to Betty Friedan and the everyday citizens who pushed the boundaries of what American democracy could be. Across seven thematic sections, it reveals a community deeply committed to the democratic experiment, even when divided on how best to achieve its promise. A timely invitation to reflect on the past and consider the future of democracy in America. Presented by the American Jewish Historical Society, the Center for Jewish History, and the Yeshiva University Museum.
